screens.title: Elastic Load Balancing (ELB) overview
screens.narratorSegment: Load balancers are the fundamental building block for scalable, fault-tolerant applications. At its core, ELB is a managed service that distributes incoming application traffic across multiple registered targets, such as EC2 instances, and spans multiple Availability Zones to avoid single points of failure. When a target becomes unhealthy, health checks configured at the target group level prevent further traffic from being routed to it. That simple behavior improves overall application availability. Consider a scenario where two instances host the same website; ELB balances client requests so no single instance is overwhelmed and users see consistent service during instance replacement or failure. A common misconception is that a load balancer alone solves all scaling issues — it does not replace autoscaling or proper instance sizing. ELB reduces the risk of overload but should be combined with autoscaling groups and capacity planning. Key signals to monitor are unhealthy host counts and request latencies per target. In practice, ELB lets you design systems where traffic is directed only to healthy endpoints, enabling rolling updates and graceful instance replacement. Reflect on your app: which parts would benefit first from ELB?

keyIdea.title: ELB in one line
keyIdea.text: Automatically distribute traffic across multiple targets and Availability Zones to increase fault tolerance and scalability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › ELB overview
Definition

Elastic Load Balancing

A managed AWS service that spreads requests across targets and AZs, and uses health checks to route only to healthy endpoints.

Benefit: Fault tolerance
Traffic moves away from unhealthy targets automatically.
Benefit: Scalability
Distribute load across many instances or containers.
Common misconception

A load balancer is not a substitute for autoscaling. ELB distributes traffic but you still need enough healthy capacity behind it. Use health checks, autoscaling policies, and monitoring together.

Illustration
Example: simple web fleet

Two EC2 instances in different AZs registered to a target group. ELB forwards incoming HTTP requests to either instance and runs health checks on path '/'.

Health check snippet
HealthCheck:
  Protocol: HTTP
  Path: /
  IntervalSeconds: 30
  TimeoutSeconds: 5
  HealthyThreshold: 3
  UnhealthyThreshold: 2
Key Takeaway

ELB helps keep users served by routing only to healthy targets and distributing traffic so no single server becomes a bottleneck.

screens.title: ALB vs NLB vs GLB
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right load balancer depends on traffic type, required features, and performance needs. Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 and is designed for HTTP and HTTPS workloads. It inspects request content, supports path- and host-based routing, and fits microservices and containerized applications with dynamic ports. A concrete example is routing api. example. com/users to a users service and api. example. com/products to a products service via listener rules. Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4 and forwards TCP, UDP, or TLS without inspecting request content. NLBs are purpose-built for extreme performance and maintain a static IP per Availability Zone, which is important when clients must whitelist IPs or when very low latency is required, such as game servers or IoT backplanes. Gateway Load Balancer focuses on deploying virtual appliances and inserting them in the network path; use it for managed firewalls or intrusion detection where you need transparent traffic redirection via Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints. A common contrast is thinking ALB is always safer; in fact, ALB adds processing and is not suitable for raw TCP needs. Choose based on protocol, performance, and whether you need content-based routing or appliance insertion. Which trade-off matters most for your app?

keyIdea.title: Decision guide
keyIdea.text: ALB for Layer 7 routing and microservices, NLB for Layer 4 performance and static IPs, GLB for virtual appliance insertion.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › ALB • NLB • GLB
ALB (Layer 7)

Content-based routing for HTTP/HTTPS

ALB matches URL paths, host headers, and methods. Ideal for microservices and containers where different paths map to different services.

Example: {host: api.example.com, path: /users} → users target group
NLB (Layer 4)

Extreme performance and static IPs

NLB forwards TCP/UDP without inspecting content. Use when latency and connection scale matter or when static IPs are required for whitelisting.

GLB (Gateway)

Insert virtual appliances

Use Gateway Load Balancer to deploy firewalls and deep packet inspection as transparent appliances using Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints.

Decision matrix
Protocol
ALB: HTTP/HTTPS. NLB: TCP/UDP/TLS. GLB: network appliances.
Use case
ALB: microservices. NLB: gaming, IoT. GLB: firewalls and IDS.
IP behavior
NLB: static per AZ. ALB: DNS-based. GLB: integrates via endpoints.
Routing
ALB: content-aware. NLB: packet forwarding. GLB: transparent appliance insertion.
Common mistake

Choosing ALB for raw TCP workloads because it feels higher-level. ALB inspects HTTP content and adds processing that is not suitable for low-level TCP/UDP workloads. Match protocol to balancer type.

Key takeaway

Select an ELB by protocol, performance need, and whether you require content-based routing or appliance insertion.

screens.title: Configuring an ALB
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring an Application Load Balancer requires a few deliberate steps and an understanding of how they work together. First, create a target group that defines the protocol and port and contains the registered targets — for example, two EC2 instances running a web server on port 80. Target groups own health checks; configure a health check path such as '/' so unhealthy instances are removed from rotation. Second, create the ALB itself and pick public subnets in at least two Availability Zones to ensure redundancy. Third, add a listener—usually HTTP or HTTPS on port 80 or 443—and set default and optional rule-based actions. Listener rules allow you to inspect the host header or URL path and forward to different target groups, enabling many applications to share a single ALB. For example, route traffic for '/users' and '/products' to separate target groups. A common pitfall is forgetting to allow the ALB security group to reach target instances' security groups; ensure the instances accept traffic from the ALB. After provisioning, test using the ALB DNS name and refresh to observe traffic distribution. Practice these steps in your lab to make them procedural and repeatable.

keyIdea.title: ALB configuration summary
keyIdea.text: Define a target group with health checks, create an ALB in multiple AZs, add listeners, and use listener rules to route by content.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Configure ALB
Step 1
Create target group

Set target type to Instances, protocol HTTP and port 80. Configure health checks on '/' so only healthy targets receive traffic.

Step 2
Provision ALB across AZs

Choose at least two public subnets and a security group that allows inbound HTTP. This ensures redundancy and high availability.

Step 3
Add listeners and rules

Add an HTTP/HTTPS listener and forward to the appropriate target group. Use path or host-based rules for microservice routing.

Key Tip

Ensure instance security groups allow traffic from the ALB security group; otherwise health checks and traffic will fail.

Example rule
Route by path
If path is /users → forward to UsersTargetGroup. If path is /products → forward to ProductsTargetGroup. Default → FrontendTargetGroup.
Check your understanding
  • Why configure health checks on the target group rather than the ALB itself?
  • What happens if the ALB security group is not allowed in the instance security group?
Test

After the ALB is active, copy its DNS name into a browser and refresh several times. You should see responses coming from both registered instances as traffic is distributed.

screens.title: Network Load Balancer (NLB)
screens.narratorSegment: Network Load Balancer operates at the transport layer and is optimized for extreme performance. Unlike ALB, NLB does not inspect HTTP content; it forwards TCP and UDP packets directly to targets. This design gives NLB ultra-low latency and the ability to handle millions of connections per second. A distinctive feature is a static IP address per Availability Zone, which helps when clients need IPs whitelisted. For example, a real-time game server that accepts many simultaneous TCP connections benefits from NLB because it reduces packet processing overhead. NLB is also commonly paired with Global Accelerator to provide a fixed entry point and optimized global routing. A common misconception is that NLB removes the need to think about security groups; you still must configure network-level controls appropriately. When choosing NLB, verify that your workload requires raw transport performance and consider whether you need static IPs for client firewall rules. The core claim to remember is: NLB is for raw, fast packet forwarding, not content-aware routing. Network Load Balancer (NLB) means layer 4 forwarding for tcp/udp with static ips per az and design for very high connection rates and low latency.. In practical terms, layer 4 forwarding for ultra-low latency and static ip needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NLB at a glance
keyIdea.text: Layer 4 forwarding for TCP/UDP with static IPs per AZ and design for very high connection rates and low latency.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Network Load Balancer
Core trait

Layer 4 packet forwarding

NLB forwards TCP/UDP/TLS with minimal processing to achieve high throughput and very low latency.

Static IPs

NLB provides a static IP per Availability Zone. Use this when clients require fixed IPs for firewall rules or whitelisting.

Example scenario
A global gaming backend accepts millions of TCP connections. NLB minimizes latency and gives a stable IP to register with game clients and partner networks.
Common pitfall

Using NLB when you need content-based routing. If you need path- or host-based decisions, choose ALB instead because NLB cannot inspect HTTP payloads.

Key Takeaway

Pick NLB for raw transport performance and static IP requirements; pick ALB when request inspection and HTTP routing are needed.

screens.title: Gateway Load Balancer (GLB)
screens.narratorSegment: Gateway Load Balancer solves the problem of deploying, scaling, and managing virtual network appliances like firewalls and intrusion detection systems. It operates at Layer 3 and Layer 4 and provides transparent insertion of third-party appliances into the data path. The key building block is the Gateway Load Balancer Endpoint, a VPC endpoint that forwards traffic to your appliance fleet without complex route changes. This architecture makes it easier to scale appliance fleets and keep traffic flows simple. Consider a managed firewall vendor deployment: GLB lets you send traffic through the vendor’s virtual appliances while maintaining standard VPC networking. A common misconception is that GLB replaces the need for explicit security configuration; it does not — you must still configure appliance policies and VPC controls. GLB’s value is in simplifying traffic steering and scaling for network functions that must inspect or transform packets. If your architecture needs deep packet inspection or inline security that can’t be achieved by ALB rules or WAF, GLB is the appropriate tool. Gateway Load Balancer (GLB) means use gateway load balancer to insert and scale virtual appliances transparently via gateway load balancer endpoints.. In practical terms, inserting network appliances into your vpc traffic path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use Gateway Load Balancer to insert and scale virtual appliances transparently via Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Gateway Load Balancer
Purpose

Virtual appliance insertion

GLB helps deploy and scale firewalls, IDS, and similar network appliances by inserting them into the traffic path using endpoints.

Key component

Gateway Load Balancer Endpoint is the VPC endpoint type that routes traffic into the appliance fleet without complex route table changes.

Example
A company inserts a managed IDS device into the VPC. Traffic to and from certain subnets flows through the GLB endpoint to the IDS appliances, which inspect packets before returning them to the path.
Misconception

GLB does not eliminate the need to configure appliance rules or VPC-level security controls. It simplifies insertion and scaling, but policies still live on the appliances.

Key takeaway

Choose GLB when you must run inline network functions that need to inspect or transform packets at scale.

screens.title: Amazon CloudFront fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon CloudFront is a global Content Delivery Network that uses edge locations, also called Points of Presence, to cache and deliver content closer to users. When a user requests an asset, CloudFront routes that request to the nearest edge location. If the content is already cached, CloudFront serves it immediately with low latency. If not, CloudFront fetches the content from your origin — an S3 static website, an ELB, or an HTTP server — caches it, and returns it to the user. This reduces latency and offloads traffic from your origin servers. CloudFront integrates with AWS WAF for security and supports custom SSL certificates. A practical example: host an index. html in an S3 bucket enabled for static website hosting and create a CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 website endpoint as the origin; the edge caches will then serve your static content quickly around the world. Common mistakes include setting TTLs too long and failing to invalidate content after updates, which can leave users seeing stale files. Remember, CloudFront is about caching and global delivery, not request-level content routing like ALB.

keyIdea.title: CloudFront in brief
keyIdea.text: A CDN that caches content at edge locations to reduce latency and origin load; ideal for static assets and accelerated delivery.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Amazon CloudFront
How it works

CloudFront serves content from the nearest edge location. If content is cached, delivery is immediate; if not, CloudFront retrieves it from the origin and caches it for subsequent requests.

Edge locations
Cache closer to users to reduce round-trip time.
Origins
S3, ELB, or any HTTP server that holds original content.
Integration

CloudFront works with AWS WAF for security and supports custom certificates. Use Origin Access Control for S3 in production for secure origin access.

Example: static site

Create an S3 bucket with static website hosting and point a CloudFront distribution to the S3 website endpoint. After deployment, the CloudFront domain serves the cached index quickly from the nearest edge.

Common mistake

Failing to invalidate or use appropriate TTLs causes visitors to receive stale assets after updates. Use invalidation or shorter TTLs during content release windows.

Key Takeaway

CloudFront speeds delivery by caching content at edge locations; configure origins and TTLs carefully to balance freshness and performance.

screens.title: Hands-on: ALB + CloudFront lab walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough ties the chapter’s concepts together with a concrete lab. Assume two EC2 instances in distinct public subnets running a simple web server on port 80. First, create a target group named MyWebServerTargetGroup using protocol HTTP and port 80. Register both instances and configure the health check on path '/'. Next, create an Application Load Balancer named MyWebAppALB, choose internet-facing, pick at least two public subnets, and attach a security group that allows HTTP from anywhere for the demo. Add a listener on port 80 and forward to your target group. Test by visiting the ALB DNS name and refreshing to see requests cycle through both instances. screens.title: Cache behavior and invalidation
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding cache behavior is critical for delivering fresh content while benefiting from CDN performance. CloudFront caches objects at edge locations according to cache policies and the TTLs you configure. Short TTLs mean frequent origin fetches and more accurate freshness but higher origin load. Long TTLs reduce origin load and improve cache hit ratios at the cost of potentially serving stale content. A typical mistake is leaving default or long TTLs during frequent content updates; that leads users to see old versions until TTLs expire. To avoid this, use invalidation requests after publishing updated assets or adopt cache-busting naming schemes such as versioned file names. CloudFront also supports caching based on query strings, headers, or cookies when necessary, but broad cache key scope reduces cache efficiency. In practice, pick conservative TTLs for dynamic assets and longer TTLs for large static assets like images and videos. Think about your content change patterns: if marketing updates images daily, plan invalidations or short TTLs during release windows. Cache behavior and invalidation means short ttls favor freshness; long ttls favor performance. use invalidation or versioned filenames to control freshness when needed.. In practical terms, how ttls, cache policies and invalidations determine freshness. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › Cache behavior
Cache policy basics

CloudFront caches objects with TTLs defined in cache policies. The origin response and distribution settings determine how long objects remain at edge locations.

Short TTL
Fresher content, higher origin load.
Long TTL
Better cache hit ratio, possible staleness.
Invalidation

Create invalidation requests for specific object paths to force edge locations to fetch the updated version from the origin before TTL expiry.

Example strategy
  • Static images: long TTL and use versioned filenames on update.
  • Marketing assets updated frequently: shorter TTLs and scheduled invalidations during releases.
  • HTML pages with dynamic fragments: use edge-side includes or keep short TTLs.
Key takeaway

Plan caching based on how often content changes. Use invalidations or versioned file names to prevent stale content from being served.

screens.title: AWS Global Accelerator
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Global Accelerator is designed to improve performance and availability for globally distributed users by providing two static Anycast IP addresses as fixed entry points into the AWS network. When a user connects to those IPs, the request is routed to the nearest AWS edge location, then traverses the AWS global network to a healthy regional endpoint such as an ALB, NLB, or EC2 instance. This differs from CloudFront, which focuses on caching static content at edge locations. Global Accelerator optimizes the route for dynamic or non-cacheable traffic, reducing latency by avoiding congested public internet paths. A concrete example is a global gaming backend where clients connect to static IPs that are whitelisted by client firewalls; Global Accelerator directs them to the nearest healthy regional endpoint and leverages AWS’s backbone for the bulk of the path. A common misconception is thinking Global Accelerator duplicates CloudFront; instead, use CloudFront for cached static assets and Global Accelerator when you need stable IPs and an accelerated path for dynamic traffic. Decide based on whether your traffic benefits from caching or from an optimized transport path.

keyIdea.title: Global Accelerator essence
keyIdea.text: Provides static Anycast IPs and routes dynamic traffic over the AWS global network to reduce latency and improve availability for global users.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.5 › AWS Global Accelerator
What it provides

Static Anycast IPs and optimized routing

Global Accelerator offers two static Anycast IPs that act as fixed entry points and route traffic via the AWS global network to the nearest healthy endpoint.

When to use

Choose Global Accelerator when you need consistent static IPs and improved routing for dynamic, non-cacheable traffic across regions.

Example

A global application uses Global Accelerator to give users a predictable IP to connect to. The service routes those connections to the nearest edge and then over AWS’s backbone to the healthy regional endpoint.

Misconception

Global Accelerator is not a caching layer. It optimizes routing for dynamic traffic; use CloudFront when you want caching at edge locations.

Key takeaway

Use Global Accelerator for static IPs and improved transport for dynamic traffic; use CloudFront for cached static content.

CloudFront

A CDN that caches and serves data from edge locations to reduce latency and speed delivery to global users.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll build a clear mental model of load balancing and content delivery on AWS. You will understand why distributing traffic matters, which load balancer types solve which problems, and when to add a CDN or Global Accelerator. Start by thinking about a single web server: when traffic increases it can become a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Elastic Load Balancing solves that by automatically spreading requests across multiple targets in multiple Availability Zones, improving fault tolerance and scalability. We’ll then look at three ELB types — Application Load Balancer for content-based routing, Network Load Balancer for extreme, low-latency TCP/UDP workloads with static IPs, and Gateway Load Balancer for inserting virtual network appliances. Next, you’ll see how CloudFront caches content at edge locations to reduce latency and how Global Accelerator provides static Anycast IPs and a predictable global network path for dynamic traffic. Along the way I’ll show concrete configuration steps you can follow in the console and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end, you’ll be able to choose the right load balancer and delivery strategy for common application scenarios. What question would you ask about your own app’s traffic pattern?

These objectives map to practical skills you’ll use when designing and operating AWS applications. First, you’ll explain the purpose and benefits of Elastic Load Balancing, which helps your application scale and tolerate failure by distributing traffic across multiple targets and Availability Zones. Second, you’ll learn to distinguish the three ELB types — Application, Network, and Gateway — and match each to real workloads. Third, you’ll configure an Application Load Balancer end-to-end: create target groups, register instances, set up listeners, and verify health checks. Fourth, you’ll understand listener rules and how content-based routing enables multiple microservices to share a single ALB. Each objective combines a conceptual explanation with an actionable outcome you can verify in the console. These competencies matter because they prevent single points of failure, improve latency for users, and let you route traffic precisely to the right service. As you study, think about which objective you’d like to practice first on a lab environment.

This page continues the objectives with a focus on high-performance delivery and appliance insertion. First, you’ll learn the Network Load Balancer’s operational characteristics: Layer 4 forwarding, static IP addresses per Availability Zone, and suitability for TCP/UDP workloads that need ultra-low latency. Second, you’ll explore Gateway Load Balancer and how it allows third-party virtual appliances like firewalls to be inserted into the packet path via Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints. Third, you’ll master Amazon CloudFront’s caching model: how edge locations cache content, how origin configuration and TTLs affect freshness, and the mechanics of invalidations. Finally, you’ll learn when AWS Global Accelerator is the right addition: when you need static Anycast IPs and an optimized AWS global transport path for dynamic, non-cacheable traffic. Each objective ties to a verifiable task — for example, creating a CloudFront distribution and testing that an edge location serves cached content — so you can confirm competency in a lab environment.

Load balancers are the fundamental building block for scalable, fault-tolerant applications. At its core, ELB is a managed service that distributes incoming application traffic across multiple registered targets, such as EC2 instances, and spans multiple Availability Zones to avoid single points of failure. When a target becomes unhealthy, health checks configured at the target group level prevent further traffic from being routed to it. That simple behavior improves overall application availability. Consider a scenario where two instances host the same website; ELB balances client requests so no single instance is overwhelmed and users see consistent service during instance replacement or failure. A common misconception is that a load balancer alone solves all scaling issues — it does not replace autoscaling or proper instance sizing. ELB reduces the risk of overload but should be combined with autoscaling groups and capacity planning. Key signals to monitor are unhealthy host counts and request latencies per target. In practice, ELB lets you design systems where traffic is directed only to healthy endpoints, enabling rolling updates and graceful instance replacement. Reflect on your app: which parts would benefit first from ELB?

Choosing the right load balancer depends on traffic type, required features, and performance needs. Application Load Balancer operates at Layer 7 and is designed for HTTP and HTTPS workloads. It inspects request content, supports path- and host-based routing, and fits microservices and containerized applications with dynamic ports. A concrete example is routing api. example. com/users to a users service and api. example. com/products to a products service via listener rules. Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4 and forwards TCP, UDP, or TLS without inspecting request content. NLBs are purpose-built for extreme performance and maintain a static IP per Availability Zone, which is important when clients must whitelist IPs or when very low latency is required, such as game servers or IoT backplanes. Gateway Load Balancer focuses on deploying virtual appliances and inserting them in the network path; use it for managed firewalls or intrusion detection where you need transparent traffic redirection via Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints. A common contrast is thinking ALB is always safer; in fact, ALB adds processing and is not suitable for raw TCP needs. Choose based on protocol, performance, and whether you need content-based routing or appliance insertion. Which trade-off matters most for your app?

Configuring an Application Load Balancer requires a few deliberate steps and an understanding of how they work together. First, create a target group that defines the protocol and port and contains the registered targets — for example, two EC2 instances running a web server on port 80. Target groups own health checks; configure a health check path such as '/' so unhealthy instances are removed from rotation. Second, create the ALB itself and pick public subnets in at least two Availability Zones to ensure redundancy. Third, add a listener—usually HTTP or HTTPS on port 80 or 443—and set default and optional rule-based actions. Listener rules allow you to inspect the host header or URL path and forward to different target groups, enabling many applications to share a single ALB. For example, route traffic for '/users' and '/products' to separate target groups. A common pitfall is forgetting to allow the ALB security group to reach target instances' security groups; ensure the instances accept traffic from the ALB. After provisioning, test using the ALB DNS name and refresh to observe traffic distribution. Practice these steps in your lab to make them procedural and repeatable.

Network Load Balancer operates at the transport layer and is optimized for extreme performance. Unlike ALB, NLB does not inspect HTTP content; it forwards TCP and UDP packets directly to targets. This design gives NLB ultra-low latency and the ability to handle millions of connections per second. A distinctive feature is a static IP address per Availability Zone, which helps when clients need IPs whitelisted. For example, a real-time game server that accepts many simultaneous TCP connections benefits from NLB because it reduces packet processing overhead. NLB is also commonly paired with Global Accelerator to provide a fixed entry point and optimized global routing. A common misconception is that NLB removes the need to think about security groups; you still must configure network-level controls appropriately. When choosing NLB, verify that your workload requires raw transport performance and consider whether you need static IPs for client firewall rules. The core claim to remember is: NLB is for raw, fast packet forwarding, not content-aware routing. Network Load Balancer (NLB) means layer 4 forwarding for tcp/udp with static ips per az and design for very high connection rates and low latency.. In practical terms, layer 4 forwarding for ultra-low latency and static ip needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Gateway Load Balancer solves the problem of deploying, scaling, and managing virtual network appliances like firewalls and intrusion detection systems. It operates at Layer 3 and Layer 4 and provides transparent insertion of third-party appliances into the data path. The key building block is the Gateway Load Balancer Endpoint, a VPC endpoint that forwards traffic to your appliance fleet without complex route changes. This architecture makes it easier to scale appliance fleets and keep traffic flows simple. Consider a managed firewall vendor deployment: GLB lets you send traffic through the vendor’s virtual appliances while maintaining standard VPC networking. A common misconception is that GLB replaces the need for explicit security configuration; it does not — you must still configure appliance policies and VPC controls. GLB’s value is in simplifying traffic steering and scaling for network functions that must inspect or transform packets. If your architecture needs deep packet inspection or inline security that can’t be achieved by ALB rules or WAF, GLB is the appropriate tool. Gateway Load Balancer (GLB) means use gateway load balancer to insert and scale virtual appliances transparently via gateway load balancer endpoints.. In practical terms, inserting network appliances into your vpc traffic path. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Amazon CloudFront is a global Content Delivery Network that uses edge locations, also called Points of Presence, to cache and deliver content closer to users. When a user requests an asset, CloudFront routes that request to the nearest edge location. If the content is already cached, CloudFront serves it immediately with low latency. If not, CloudFront fetches the content from your origin — an S3 static website, an ELB, or an HTTP server — caches it, and returns it to the user. This reduces latency and offloads traffic from your origin servers. CloudFront integrates with AWS WAF for security and supports custom SSL certificates. A practical example: host an index. html in an S3 bucket enabled for static website hosting and create a CloudFront distribution that uses the S3 website endpoint as the origin; the edge caches will then serve your static content quickly around the world. Common mistakes include setting TTLs too long and failing to invalidate content after updates, which can leave users seeing stale files. Remember, CloudFront is about caching and global delivery, not request-level content routing like ALB.
